title: Student Record System
description:
### Problem Statement
Structures in C (`struct`) allow programmers to group logically related variables of different types into a single composite entity. Managing arrays of structures is a cornerstone of data processing in systems programming. In this problem, you will implement a Student Record Management system supporting CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on an array of `Student` structures.

#### Structure Definition:
```c
typedef struct {
    int id;
    char name[32];
    float gpa;
} Student;
```

#### Supported Operations:
1. `ADD <id> <name> <gpa>`:
   - Check if a student with `<id>` already exists in the system.
   - If already present, print `ALREADY_EXISTS`.
   - Otherwise, append the new student to the records and print `ADDED`.
2. `FIND <id>`:
   - Search for a student by `<id>`.
   - If found, print `<name> <gpa>` where GPA is formatted to 2 decimal places (`%.2f`).
   - If not found, print `NOT_FOUND`.
3. `DELETE <id>`:
   - Search for a student by `<id>`.
   - If found, remove the student, preserve or pack the array, and print `DELETED`.
   - If not found, print `NOT_FOUND`.
4. `UPDATE <id> <new_gpa>`:
   - Find student by `<id>`.
   - If found, update their GPA to `<new_gpa>` and print `UPDATED`.
   - If not found, print `NOT_FOUND`.
5. `TOP`:
   - Find the student with the highest GPA.
   - If multiple students share the exact highest GPA, select the one with the smallest numerical `<id>`.
   - Print `<name> <gpa>` formatted to 2 decimal places.
   - If the system contains no student records, print `EMPTY`.

Process $N$ operations sequentially from standard input.
input_format:
The first line contains N (number of operations).
The next N lines each contain an operation command: ADD <id> <name> <gpa>, FIND <id>, DELETE <id>, UPDATE <id> <gpa>, or TOP.
output_format: Print the result of each operation on a new line.

examples.input:
7
ADD 101 Alice 3.85
ADD 102 Bob 3.92
FIND 101
TOP
UPDATE 101 3.95
TOP
DELETE 102
examples.output:
ADDED
ADDED
Alice 3.85
Bob 3.92
UPDATED
Alice 3.95
DELETED
examples.explanation: Alice and Bob are added. Bob is top with 3.92. Alice is updated to 3.95, making her top. Bob is then deleted.

examples.input:
5
TOP
FIND 999
DELETE 999
UPDATE 999 4.0
ADD 1 John 3.50
examples.explanation: Querying empty system outputs EMPTY. Looking up or deleting non-existent IDs yields NOT_FOUND.

hints: Use an array of Student structs and maintain an integer count of active records.
Write a helper function find_index(sys, id) that returns the index or -1.
When deleting an element at index i, shift records from i + 1 to count - 1 left by one position.
For TOP, break GPA ties by selecting the student with the smaller id.
explanation: Struct arrays allow storing heterogenous data attributes together in contiguous memory. Linear scanning through the records provides O(N) lookup and deletion, while maintaining an array count avoids tracking sentinel records.
time_complexity: O(N) for ADD, FIND, DELETE, UPDATE, TOP operations where N is the current student count
common_mistakes: Using == comparison on floating-point GPAs without considering equality tie-breaking rules.
Leaving gaps in the array after deletion rather than shifting subsequent elements.
Not checking whether a student ID already exists prior to adding.

test_cases.input:
7
ADD 101 Alice 3.85
ADD 102 Bob 3.92
FIND 101
TOP
UPDATE 101 3.95
TOP
DELETE 102
test_cases.expected_output:

ADDED
Alice 3.85
Bob 3.92
UPDATED
Alice 3.95
DELETED
test_cases.description: Standard ADD, FIND, UPDATE, TOP, and DELETE operations

TOP

title: Sort Structures by Multiple Fields
input_format:
The first line contains N (number of candidates).
The next N lines each contain name, score, and age separated by spaces.
output_format: Print N lines of sorted candidates in the format '<name> <score> <age>'.

examples.explanation: Bob has highest score (90). Alice, Charlie, and David tie at 85. Charlie and David are younger (19) than Alice (20). Charlie precedes David alphabetically.
All candidates have score 100 and age 25. Lexicographical order yields Aaron, Ben, then Zara.

hints: Cast the void pointers: const Candidate *c1 = (const Candidate *)a;
For descending score: if (c1->score != c2->score) return c2->score - c1->score;
For ascending age: if (c1->age != c2->age) return c1->age - c2->age;
Use strcmp(c1->name, c2->name) as the final tie-breaker.
explanation: Multi-field sorting in C relies on qsort with chained conditionals. If field A differs, return the difference immediately; if equal, fall through to field B, and finally to strcmp on field C. qsort executes in O(N log N) average time.
time_complexity: O(N log N) using standard library quicksort
space_complexity: O(N) to store the candidate array
common_mistakes: Inverting the order for descending vs ascending fields (e.g. c1 - c2 instead of c2 - c1).
Returning 0 prematurely before checking remaining tie-breaking fields.
Failing to cast const void * correctly to const Candidate *.

test_cases.description: Score tie-breaking with age, and age tie-breaking with name
All scores and ages identical; purely alphabetical sort
Strictly descending scores without ties
Single element array

title: Structure Pointer Linked List
input_format:
The first line contains Q (number of commands).

common_mistakes: Dereferencing a freed pointer: accessing curr->next after calling free(curr).

title: Union Memory Layout Analyzer
description:
### Problem Statement
Unlike a `struct` where each member has its own distinct offset in memory, all members of a `union` in C share the **exact same starting memory address**. The total size of a union is determined by the size of its largest member (plus any alignment padding). Writing to one member overwrites the raw bytes of all other members. In systems programming, unions are used for low-level packet decoding, hardware register manipulation, and type punning.

In this problem, you will analyze the memory overlay and little-endian representation of a 4-byte multi-view union:
```c
typedef union {
    uint32_t u32;
    uint16_t u16[2];
    uint8_t u8[4];
} MultiView;
```

#### Endianness Note:
Standard modern architectures (x86_64, ARM64) use **little-endian** byte ordering. The least significant byte (LSB) is stored at byte index `0` (`u8[0]`), and the most significant byte (MSB) is stored at byte index `3` (`u8[3]`).
Similarly:
- `u16[0]` comprises bytes `u8[0]` (low) and `u8[1]` (high).
- `u16[1]` comprises bytes `u8[2]` (low) and `u8[3]` (high).

#### Supported Commands:
1. `SET_U32 <hex>`: Set `u32` to the given 32-bit unsigned hex value (e.g. `0x12345678`). Print `OK`.
2. `SET_BYTE <idx> <hex>`: Set byte `u8[idx]` to the given 8-bit hex value ($0 \le \text{val} \le 255$).
   - If `<idx> < 0` or `<idx> > 3`, print `OUT_OF_BOUNDS`.
   - Otherwise, update the byte and print `OK`.
3. `SHOW_BYTES`: Print the 4 bytes in hex from index 0 to 3:
   `B0:0x%02X B1:0x%02X B2:0x%02X B3:0x%02X`
4. `SHOW_U16`: Print the two 16-bit words in hex:
   `W0:0x%04X W1:0x%04X`
5. `SHOW_U32`: Print the 32-bit integer in hex and unsigned decimal:
   `HEX:0x%08X DEC:%u`
input_format:
The first line contains N (number of operations).
The next N lines each contain a command: SET_U32 <hex>, SET_BYTE <idx> <hex>, SHOW_BYTES, SHOW_U16, or SHOW_U32.
output_format: Print the response for each command on a separate line.
constraints:
1 <= N <= 200
-10 <= idx <= 10
Hex values provided without '0x' prefix for scanf (%x)

examples.input:
5
SET_U32 12345678
SHOW_BYTES
SHOW_U16
SHOW_U32
SET_BYTE 0 FF
examples.explanation: Setting 0x12345678 on a little-endian machine places 0x78 at byte 0, 0x56 at byte 1, 0x34 at byte 2, and 0x12 at byte 3. W0 combines byte 0 and 1 (0x5678).

examples.input:
4
SHOW_BYTES
SET_BYTE 4 AA
SET_BYTE -1 BB
SHOW_U32
examples.output:
B0:0x00 B1:0x00 B2:0x00 B3:0x00
OUT_OF_BOUNDS
OUT_OF_BOUNDS
HEX:0x00000000 DEC:0
examples.explanation: Initially zeroed. Byte indices < 0 or > 3 are rejected with OUT_OF_BOUNDS.

hints: In C, union members share the same starting address.
Use scanf("%x", &val) to parse hexadecimal inputs.
Remember that in little-endian, byte 0 is the least significant byte.
Print using uppercase hex formatting: %02X, %04X, %08X.
explanation: Unions enable type punning and multi-view representation of memory buffers. On little-endian architectures, the lowest-order byte of a multi-byte scalar is stored at the lowest memory address. Manipulating individual bytes immediately reflects across all larger union members.
common_mistakes: Assuming big-endian ordering where byte 0 would hold the most significant byte.
Forgetting to check bounds on byte index (0 <= idx <= 3).
Using signed integer formatters (%d) instead of unsigned (%u) for 32-bit values exceeding INT_MAX.

test_cases.input:
5
SET_U32 12345678
SHOW_BYTES
SHOW_U16
SHOW_U32
SET_BYTE 0 FF
test_cases.description: Little-endian byte layout of 0x12345678 and byte mutation

test_cases.input:
4
SHOW_BYTES
SET_BYTE 4 AA
SET_BYTE -1 BB
SHOW_U32
test_cases.expected_output:

OUT_OF_BOUNDS
OUT_OF_BOUNDS

W0:0xFFFF W1:0xFFFF
HEX:0xFFFFFFFF DEC:4294967295
test_cases.description: All bits set (0xFFFFFFFF)

test_cases.input:

SET_BYTE 2 00
SHOW_BYTES
SHOW_U16

OK

title: Enum-Based State Machine
description:
### Problem Statement
Enumerations (`enum`) in C define user-friendly symbolic names for integral constants. They are extensively used in embedded systems and driver programming to implement **Finite State Machines (FSMs)**. A state machine maintains a current state and evaluates incoming events to trigger state transitions and associated actions.

In this problem, you will model a vending machine controller using C `enum`s.

#### State Definitions:
```c
typedef enum {
    STATE_IDLE,
    STATE_COIN_INSERTED
} VendingState;
```

#### Machine Variables:
- `state`: Current state, starts at `STATE_IDLE`.
- `stock`: Current inventory count of the item, initialized from input.
- `balance`: Total cents inserted in the current transaction, initially `0`.
- **Item Price:** Fixed at `50` cents per item.

#### Events & Rules:
1. `INSERT <amount>`:
   - `<amount>` is in cents ($> 0$).
   - Add `<amount>` to `balance`.
   - Transition to `STATE_COIN_INSERTED`.
   - Print `BALANCE: <balance> STATE: COIN_INSERTED`.
2. `SELECT`:
   - If `state == STATE_IDLE`: print `INVALID_ACTION`.
   - If `state == STATE_COIN_INSERTED`:
     - If `stock == 0`: Out of stock! Refund entire `balance`, set `balance = 0`, transition to `STATE_IDLE`, and print `OUT_OF_STOCK REFUND: <refund_amount> STATE: IDLE`.
     - Else if `balance < 50`: Insufficient funds. Print `INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS NEED: <50 - balance>`.
     - Else (`balance >= 50` and `stock > 0`):
       - Dispense item: decrement `stock` by 1.
       - Calculate change = `balance - 50`.
       - Print `DISPENSING CHANGE: <change>`.
       - Set `balance = 0`, transition to `STATE_IDLE`.
3. `REFUND`:
   - If `state == STATE_COIN_INSERTED`:
     - Refund all inserted coins.
     - Print `REFUND: <balance> STATE: IDLE`.
     - Set `balance = 0`, transition to `STATE_IDLE`.
   - Else (`state == STATE_IDLE`):
     - Print `NO_COINS`.
4. `RESTOCK <count>`:
   - Increase `stock` by `<count>`.
   - Print `STOCK: <stock>`.
input_format:
The first line contains initial_stock.
The second line contains N (number of commands).
The following N lines each contain a command: INSERT <amount>, SELECT, REFUND, or RESTOCK <count>.
output_format: Print the response for each command on a separate line.

examples.input:
2
6
INSERT 25
SELECT
INSERT 50
SELECT
REFUND
RESTOCK 5
examples.output:
BALANCE: 25 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS NEED: 25
BALANCE: 75 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
DISPENSING CHANGE: 25
NO_COINS
STOCK: 6
examples.explanation: Inserting 25 gives 25 cents. Selecting reports 25 more needed. Adding 50 makes balance 75. Selecting dispenses item (cost 50), returning 25 cents change and resetting state to IDLE.

examples.output:
INVALID_ACTION
NO_COINS
BALANCE: 100 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
OUT_OF_STOCK REFUND: 100 STATE: IDLE
examples.explanation: When stock is 0, selecting after inserting coins triggers OUT_OF_STOCK, refunds all inserted coins, and returns machine to IDLE.

hints: Use enum for states: typedef enum { STATE_IDLE, STATE_COIN_INSERTED } VendingState;
Check current state before executing actions: SELECT when IDLE is an INVALID_ACTION.
Remember that dispensing item sets balance to 0 and transitions state back to STATE_IDLE.
When out of stock, refund the current balance before zeroing it out.
explanation: State machines control transitions between distinct operating modes. Enums provide compile-time type safety and readable symbolic constants. State-based conditionals prevent illegal operations (like selecting an item without inserting coins).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to transition state back to STATE_IDLE after dispensing an item or issuing a refund.
Not zeroing out the balance after dispensing or refunding.
Failing to handle stock == 0 when SELECT is called.

test_cases.input:
2
6
INSERT 25
SELECT
INSERT 50
SELECT
REFUND
RESTOCK 5
test_cases.expected_output:
BALANCE: 25 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS NEED: 25
BALANCE: 75 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
DISPENSING CHANGE: 25
NO_COINS
STOCK: 6
test_cases.description: Insufficient funds, subsequent coin insertion, dispensing with change, restock

NO_COINS

BALANCE: 50 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
DISPENSING CHANGE: 0

OUT_OF_STOCK REFUND: 50 STATE: IDLE

test_cases.description: Depleting stock to zero on second purchase

test_cases.expected_output:

BALANCE: 30 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
REFUND: 30 STATE: IDLE
NO_COINS
test_cases.description: Accumulating multiple coin inserts and canceling with refund

BALANCE: 50 STATE: COIN_INSERTED
DISPENSING CHANGE: 0
test_cases.description: Restocking before purchase and exact payment (0 change)

title: Typedef and Function Pointer Dispatch
description:
### Problem Statement
In systems software, operating system kernels, and device driver frameworks, runtime command routing is often implemented using **function pointer dispatch tables** rather than large `switch` statements. This architectural pattern combines `typedef` function signatures with an array of mapping structures, decoupling command parsing from business logic.

Define the function pointer type and dispatch table entry as follows:
```c
typedef int (*OpFunc)(int a, int b, int *error_code);

typedef struct {
    char name[16];
    OpFunc func;
} CommandEntry;
```

#### Supported Operations:
1. `ADD a b`: Return $a + b$.
2. `SUB a b`: Return $a - b$.
3. `MUL a b`: Return $a \times b$.
4. `DIV a b`: Integer division $a / b$. If $b == 0$, set `*error_code = 1`.
5. `MOD a b`: Modulo $a \% b$. If $b == 0$, set `*error_code = 1`.
6. `AND a b`: Bitwise AND $a \ \& \ b$.
7. `OR a b`: Bitwise OR $a \ | \ b$.
8. `XOR a b`: Bitwise XOR $a \ \hat{} \ b$.

#### Error Handling Rules:
- If the operation name is not found in the dispatch table, print `ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP`.
- If an operation sets `*error_code != 0` (e.g. division or modulo by zero), print `ERROR: DIVISION_BY_ZERO`.
- Otherwise, print the integer result.
input_format:
The first line contains N (number of commands).
The following N lines each contain: <op> <a> <b>.
output_format: Print the integer result or error string on a new line.
constraints:
1 <= N <= 500
-10^6 <= a, b <= 10^6
Operation name length <= 15 chars

examples.input:
6
ADD 10 20
SUB 50 15
MUL 6 7
DIV 42 6
MOD 29 5
XOR 12 25
examples.explanation: Each command is looked up in the dispatch table and executed. XOR 12 (1100b) with 25 (11001b) gives 21 (10101b).

examples.output:
ERROR: DIVISION_BY_ZERO
ERROR: DIVISION_BY_ZERO
ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP
ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP
examples.explanation: b == 0 for DIV and MOD triggers error code 1. POW and SQRT are not in the table, producing ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP.

hints: Use typedef int (*OpFunc)(int a, int b, int *error_code); for the function signature.
Store command names and function pointers in an array of structs.
Loop over the dispatch table comparing names using strcmp.
Pass an error code pointer (&err) into the dispatched function to check for division by zero.
explanation: Function pointers in C provide runtime polymorphism and table-driven routing. Storing function pointers in a dispatch table avoids monolithic switch-case statements, makes adding new commands trivial (open-closed principle), and mirrors how virtual method tables (vtables) work internally.
time_complexity: O(K) search per query where K is number of registered commands (O(1) effectively)
common_mistakes: Calling free() or treating function pointers as dynamic heap memory.
Forgetting to check b == 0 in both DIV and MOD.
Dereferencing a NULL function pointer when a command is not found.

test_cases.input:
6
ADD 10 20
SUB 50 15
MUL 6 7
DIV 42 6
MOD 29 5
XOR 12 25
test_cases.description: Standard arithmetic and bitwise operations

test_cases.expected_output:
ERROR: DIVISION_BY_ZERO
ERROR: DIVISION_BY_ZERO
ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP
ERROR: UNKNOWN_OP
test_cases.description: Division by zero errors and unknown command rejection
Bitwise operations with zero operands
Negative numbers in arithmetic and modulo
Zeros as numerators and unknown op fallback

title: Structure Padding Calculator
description:
### Problem Statement
In C, the size of a structure is frequently larger than the mathematical sum of its member sizes. To optimize memory bus transfers and avoid unaligned memory access faults, compilers insert **padding bytes** between structure members and at the end of the structure (tail padding).

The standard natural alignment rules on 64-bit systems are:
1. **Member Sizes & Alignments:**
   - `char`: Size 1 byte, Alignment 1 byte.
   - `short`: Size 2 bytes, Alignment 2 bytes.
   - `int`: Size 4 bytes, Alignment 4 bytes.
   - `float`: Size 4 bytes, Alignment 4 bytes.
   - `double`: Size 8 bytes, Alignment 8 bytes.
   - `long_long`: Size 8 bytes, Alignment 8 bytes.
   - `pointer`: Size 8 bytes, Alignment 8 bytes.
2. **Placement Rule:**
   - The structure begins at offset `0`.
   - A member of alignment $A$ must be positioned at an offset that is an integer multiple of $A$. If the current offset is not a multiple of $A$, padding bytes must be inserted immediately preceding the member:
     $$\text{padding} = (A - (\text{offset} \% A)) \% A$$
   - The member then occupies `size` bytes, advancing the offset to $\text{offset} + \text{padding} + \text{size}$.
3. **Structure Alignment & Tail Padding:**
   - The alignment requirement of the entire struct ($A_{\text{struct}}$) is equal to the **maximum alignment** among all its members (or `1` if the struct has 0 members).
   - The total size of the struct must be rounded up to the nearest multiple of $A_{\text{struct}}$ by appending tail padding:
     $$\text{tail\_padding} = (A_{\text{struct}} - (\text{final\_offset} \% A_{\text{struct}})) \% A_{\text{struct}}$$

Given a sequential list of $M$ field types declared in a struct, compute the offset and padding for each member, along with the total size, total padding, and alignment.
input_format:
The first line contains M (number of field types).
The next M lines each contain a type name: char, short, int, float, double, long_long, or pointer.
output_format:
For each field, print: FIELD <i>: <type> OFFSET: <off> PAD: <pad>
Finally, print: TOTAL_SIZE: <size> TOTAL_PADDING: <pad> ALIGNMENT: <align>
constraints:
1 <= M <= 50
Supported types: char, short, int, float, double, long_long, pointer

FIELD 0: char OFFSET: 0 PAD: 0
FIELD 1: int OFFSET: 4 PAD: 3
FIELD 2: short OFFSET: 8 PAD: 0
TOTAL_SIZE: 12 TOTAL_PADDING: 5 ALIGNMENT: 4
examples.explanation: char starts at 0 (size 1). int requires 4-byte alignment, so 3 padding bytes advance offset to 4. int ends at 8. short requires 2-byte alignment (8 is a multiple of 2, pad 0) and ends at 10. Max align is 4, so 2 bytes of tail padding bring total size to 12.

hints: Formula for padding: int pad = (align - (offset % align)) % align;
Offset of the member is current_offset + pad.
Remember that max_alignment = max(max_alignment, member_alignment).
Tail padding rounds the final offset up to the nearest multiple of max_alignment.
explanation: Natural memory alignment mandates that N-byte data types reside at addresses divisible by N. The compiler inserts padding between fields to satisfy member alignment and appends tail padding to ensure array indexing of structs preserves alignment for all subsequent array elements.
common_mistakes: Forgetting tail padding at the end of the structure.
Incorrect padding formula when offset % align == 0 (without outer modulo % align).
Not tracking the maximum alignment across all members.
